 Goldman Sachs sees RBI raising repo rate to 6.25% by mid-2027 as inflation crosses 6%
 #Taxation & Finance News #Commercial #India 
 Last Updated : 30 minutes ago 
 Share 
 Font size 
 ABC Small 
 ABC Medium 
 ABC Large 
 Save 
 Print 
 Comment 
 Synopsis
 Goldman Sachs Research expects the Reserve Bank of India to raise the repo rate by a total of 75 basis points by the April–June quarter of 2027, starting with a 25-basis-point increase next month. The brokerage linked its forecast to rising food prices and inflation spreading across goods and services. It sees India’s GDP growth easing to 7.2 per cent in 2027 from an estimated 7.9 per cent this year. It has also forecast the rupee weakening to 96 against the US dollar within a year and upgraded Indian equities to overweight. 
 Representative image
 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may raise its benchmark interest rate by 75 basis points by the second quarter of calendar year 2027, as higher food prices and wider inflation pressures push the central bank towards further tightening, according to a Goldman Sachs Research report released on Wednesday. 
Goldman Sachs expects the RBI to raise the repo rate by 25 basis points in December, followed by another 50 basis points in the first half of 2027. This would take the rate to 6.25 per cent by the April–June quarter of 2027. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is scheduled to meet from December 2 to 4, with the following meeting set for February 3 to 5, 2027. 
The RBI raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent in its October policy last month, its first hike in nearly four years. At the same meeting, the MPC changed its stance from neutral to calibrated tightening, and raised its FY27 GDP growth forecast to 7.1 per cent and its CPI inflation projection to 5.2 per cent. 
The latest report brings forward Goldman’s expected timeline. In early October, Goldman Sachs Chief India Economist Santanu Sengupta had said the RBI was likely to deliver three more hikes by June 2027, with one in February, a pause to assess conditions, and a final hike in April or June. 
According to the report, headline inflation is likely to stay slightly above 6 per cent through the October–December 2026 and January–March 2027 quarters. With price pressures spreading across core goods and services, the brokerage expects the RBI to continue its calibrated tightening cycle. 
Sengupta said inflation has already crossed the upper end of the RBI’s target band, reaching 6.1 per cent last month. He expects it to stay around 6 per cent over the next two quarters before gradually easing towards the early 5 per cent range by the end of the year. Goldman Sachs expects retail inflation to average 5.7 per cent in 2027, with core inflation at 4.7 per cent, driven by higher food prices, El Nino-related weather disruptions and elevated input costs. Sengupta had earlier also flagged lower reservoir levels and crude oil prices staying above USD 100 as risks to inflation and growth. 
Despite the rate hikes, the brokerage expects GDP growth to remain strong at 7.2 per cent in 2027, down from an estimated 7.9 per cent in 2026. The report said strong domestic demand, steady private consumption and a new investment cycle in energy, materials and strategic manufacturing would support activity. However, tighter financial conditions, higher corporate borrowing costs and the fading effect of tax cuts could slow consumption and investment growth. Real investment growth is projected at around 8.5 per cent in 2027, backed by sectors linked to energy security, defence and supply-chain priorities. 
On the external front, the current account deficit is expected to stay at around 1 per cent of GDP in both 2026 and 2027, supported by services exports and remittances. The report forecast the rupee at 94, 95 and 96 against the USD over the next three, six and 12 months, respectively. 
On the Union Budget 2027-28, Sengupta said the government would continue on its fiscal consolidation path, and that capital expenditure allocation would remain broadly constant as a share of GDP. 
Goldman Sachs also upgraded India to overweight and set a Nifty target of 28,500 by the end of 2027, citing expected mid-teen earnings growth, strong domestic demand and relatively low foreign investor positioning. It said India remains an attractive option for investors looking to diversify amid uncertainty in global markets linked to artificial intelligence. 
Most floating-rate home loans in India are linked to the repo rate through external benchmarks, so further hikes would reach borrowers’ EMIs soon after each policy change. Developers could also see higher costs on construction finance at a time when input prices are already rising. Not all forecasters expect a cycle this steep. Nomura, for instance, had argued that the RBI may limit hikes to 25–50 basis points in the current cycle, saying markets were pricing in a sharper rise than the inflation outlook justified. The December policy will show which view holds.
